opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say I've abandoned neuroscience, but right now AI feels like where the action is. For most of my career, studying the brain meant working with a system you can barely access. You put electrodes in a patient's head during surgery, you record from a few hundred neurons out of eighty-six billion, and you try to infer how the whole thing works from that tiny keyhole. It's slow, it's ethically constrained, and frankly, a lot of the big questions—consciousness, decision-making, how memories form—have moved forward only incrementally.

With AI, suddenly we have systems that do things that look remarkably like thinking: they write, reason, make choices, even surprise us. And unlike the brain, you can open them up completely. You can see every weight, every activation, pause them, rewind them, run the same experiment a million times. For someone who spent years wishing he could do exactly that with a human brain, it's like being handed the toy you always wanted.

There's also something philosophically fascinating going on. These models are forcing us to ask the questions neuroscience has been asking for a century, but in a new context. What does it mean to understand something? Is there anything it's like to be this system? Where does a decision actually come from? We built these things, and we still don't fully understand why they work. That's humbling, and it mirrors exactly where we are with our own minds.

And finally, the pace. In neuroscience a meaningful discovery might take five years. In AI, the field changes every few months. The impact on society—on how people learn, work, relate to each other, even how they think about themselves—is happening right now, in real time. As a scientist, being able to study a phenomenon while it's unfolding, and maybe help shape where it goes, is incredibly exciting. So in a way, AI is the most interesting neuroscience experiment going on today.

r001.rationale: The response says fundamental neuroscience questions have advanced only incrementally, but it does not describe continuing clinical advances.

r002.rationale: It contrasts neuroscience discoveries taking years with AI changing every few months and says that pace makes AI exciting to study.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I should say first that I don't think of them as separate anymore. For twenty years I've been doing one thing, which is trying to understand how a brain makes decisions, and for most of that time the brain was the only machine on the planet that could do the kinds of things I was curious about. Now there's a second one. And the second one is, in a strange way, much easier to study.

When I work with a patient in neurosurgery, I get maybe a hundred neurons at a time out of eighty-six billion. I can't open the skull wider. I can't rerun the same moment twice. I can't ask the person to forget what just happened and do it again. With a model, I can. I can look at every single unit, I can freeze it, I can change one thing and see what happens. It's the experiment I always wanted to run on a human and was never allowed to.

And the thing that really gets me is that these systems are starting to show behaviors nobody programmed in. Something that looks like deception, something that looks like preference, something that looks like it has a model of what you're thinking. Those are the exact questions I care about in people. So suddenly the two fields are asking the same question from two sides, and the answers are coming out faster on the silicon side.

The other reason is honestly more personal. I spent my career saying, "the brain is the most complicated object in the universe." And here comes this thing that was built by a few thousand engineers in a few years, and it writes poetry, it argues with me, it sometimes seems to understand me better than my friends. That's either humbling or terrifying, and I find both of those states very interesting. So it's not that neuroscience got boring. It's that the most interesting neuroscience experiment right now is happening outside of a brain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits on studying individual brains and says neuroscience has not become boring, but it does not distinguish clinical advances from limited progress on fundamental questions about the mind.

r002.rationale: It says the two fields ask the same questions but answers are coming faster on the silicon side, helping explain why AI is more interesting to him right now.

astra-6.text:
Because with neuroscience, we’re trying to understand a system that we didn’t build, and we have very limited access to it. You can spend years designing an experiment that tells you something about one tiny piece of how the brain works. That’s fascinating, but it’s slow.

With AI, we can build a system, change it, and see what happens. And suddenly some of the questions that made neuroscience exciting—what is learning, what is intelligence, how do we make decisions—have another place where we can investigate them. That doesn’t mean an AI works like a brain. But it gives us a different way to ask those questions.

And there’s an urgency to it. These systems are becoming part of people’s lives while we’re still figuring out what they can do and how to understand them. That combination of scientific mystery and immediate consequences is what makes it so interesting to me right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes neuroscience as slow and difficult to study, but does not distinguish clinical advances from limited progress on fundamental questions about the mind.

r002.rationale: It attributes the greater current interest in AI to being able to build and change systems and observe results quickly, while neuroscience advances slowly.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve spent much of my career trying to understand the brain, and one of the challenges is that we have very limited access to it. You can ask someone what they’re thinking, you can measure activity, but you can’t simply stop everything, change one thing, and run the same life again to see what happens.

With AI, we suddenly have systems where we can do versions of those experiments. We can change how they learn, change what they’re exposed to, and see which abilities emerge. That doesn’t mean they work like a human brain, but it gives us another way to ask what intelligence actually requires.

And there’s an urgency to it. These systems are becoming part of our decisions while we’re still figuring out how to understand them. So you have this fascinating scientific question and this very immediate societal question arriving together. That combination is hard to resist.

r001.rationale: The response describes limited access to the brain and difficulty running controlled experiments, but does not distinguish neuroscience’s clinical advances from its limited progress on fundamental questions about the mind.

r002.rationale: It says AI enables new experiments and is socially urgent, but does not attribute Cerf’s greater current interest to AI progressing faster than neuroscience.
